To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) larger menus are worse than smaller menus in the 401(k) context, and 2) this can be explained by the fact that menu setters differ in menu setting ability.
smaller menus are better and that menu size and menu ability are negatively related.

(i) when the menu size increases, the menu quality decreases; (ii) the menu quality is negatively correlated with the menu size; and (iii) the optimal menu size is negatively related to menu-setter’s ability.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a fundamental trade-off between menu size and quality.
a fundamental question: what is the optimal size of a menu?
the optimal design of menus in settings where menu setters have limited menu-setting ability.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the optimal menu is not always the largest menu.
the optimal menu size is a function of the menu setter’s ability to pre-select a menu, and that a larger menu size does not guarantee better menu performance.
smaller menus are better when they are offered by a higher ability menu setter.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the optimal menu size depends on the menu setter's ability.
menu size and menu design should be tailored to the menu setter's menu setting ability, rather than to the choosers' ability to choose from the menu.
the size of the menu is not necessarily a good proxy of menu quality, as the quality of the menu depends on the menu setter's ability.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the optimal menu size is not always larger than the optimal menu size offered by an individual menu setter.
when the cost to increase menu size is low, the menu setter’s ability to pre-select items is an important factor to consider when determining the optimal menu size.
menu setters should be aware of the trade-offs between menu size and quality, and not simply focus on the number of menu options offered.
